blocks.text: Since it is clear from this that the east wind is related to the south wind, in David קדים Kadim and תימן Theman, that is, the east wind and the south wind, could be taken as synonyms, so that in this passage Kadim is nothing other than the following Theman. And not only here but frequently elsewhere the sacred writers attribute to the wind Kadim things that seem rather to be proper to the south wind. For it scorches the crops, Gen. XLI, 6. It also scorches vines and the fruits of trees, Ezech. XVII, 10. and XIX, 12. It dries up the waters of the sea and of springs, Exod. XIV, 21. and Os. XIII, 15. By its force it shatters ships, [col. 103] Psal. XLVIII, 8. and Ezech. XXVII, 26. Finally, it overturns and scatters everything, Iob. XXVII, 21. and Ierem. XVIII, 17. Accordingly it is called a harsh wind, Es. XXVII, 8. and חרשית, making people deaf with its roar, Ion. IV, 8. Nor is it anywhere called Εὖρος [Euros] by the Greeks, but Νότος [Notos] or Καύσων [Kausōn], that is, the south wind and the burning wind. And God's words in Deut. XXXII, 22. A fire is kindled in my anger, and it shall burn to the lowest hell, and shall consume the earth and its produce, Jonathan and Onkelos refer to this same wind by this paraphrase of theirs, קדום תקיף כאשא, An east wind, strong as fire, has gone out from me in anger, etc. Finally, Theodoret compares the east wind and the south wind as similar winds, almost the same, when he writes in Question 8 on Genesis, Εὔρου ἢ Νότου πνέοντος, τὸ πεπηγὸς ὕδωρ διαλύεσθαι [Eurou ē Notou pneontos, to pepēgos hydōr dialyesthai], When the east wind or the south wind blows, frozen water is dissolved. Therefore, although רוח הקדים, properly and strictly speaking, means the east wind (as both the origin of the word shows and the passage Ezech. XLII, 16. etc., where the north, south and west winds are distinguished from the wind Kadim), nevertheless, because the winds Kadim and Theman, that is, the east wind and the south wind, have certain things in common, I think the Hebrews used these words interchangeably. And hence it is that קדים Kadim is frequently rendered Νότος [Notos] by the Greeks: as in Exod. X, 13. and XIV, 21. Num. XXXIV, 15. Iob. XXXVIII, 24. Ezech. XXVII, 26. and in that very passage of the Psalm with which we are dealing, where they render Kadim and Theman as Νότον καὶ Λίβα [Noton kai Liba]. Therefore the same wind seems to be meant by both words [II, 665], namely the south wind or the south-west wind ^{(6)}, which brought the quails to the Israelites from the interior of Egypt ^{(7)}.
